jacket_copy: Highkettle pays for winter in iron. Each midwinter the mountain hamlet must carry a village relic and a tithe of metal down to the valley Hold, or lose the pass and the grain-right that keep it alive. Three weeks before the rite, raiders from poorer slopes take the relic and leave the unfinished iron. The hamlet sends Willa, the smith's grown apprentice, to walk the high pass and bring the piece back. She is sure at the anvil and on a hard path, and she is not sure what she owes Orren, the master who raised her. The crossing will cost time she does not have. The object she recovers will have a weight a smith can read. The Hold will not test what it is given unless the object is challenged. Someone must decide what is owed before the presentation ground, and the bill will not wait.

s01.text: Willa, grown apprentice to Highkettle's only smith Orren, lives in the forge-house that raised her and cannot settle what she owes him.

s02.text: Each midwinter the poor hamlet must present a village relic and a tithe of iron to the valley Hold or forfeit a year of pass-protection and winter grain-right.

s03.text: Three weeks before the rite, raiders from poorer unprotected slopes steal the relic from the village chest and leave the unfinished tithe-iron because they cannot carry both.

s04.text: Without the relic the Hold will close the pass and withhold grain, and the hamlet has no reserve of food, coin, or fighters.

s05.text: Willa's task is to retrieve the relic on foot and have it at the midwinter ground on time, with no mount, guide, or spare days.

s06.text: They send her rather than Orren because the tithe is short, he cannot make the crossing, and a woman on the path is less likely to be met as a fighter.

s07.text: The pass exacts cold and walking time she cannot spare, and the raiders are hungry people, not an army.

s08.text: She finds their camp, takes the relic by stealth and craft judgment, and does not kill for a village object.

s09.text: The crossing costs her the hours when Orren might have spoken first, and a frost injury that will still mark her hands at the rite.

s10.text: Before she sleeps she reads the relic as a smith and finds the wrong weight, Orren's forty-year weld, and an inclusion where a living levy sits.

s11.text: She takes the reading to him, and he does not deny forging the piece and binding the levy to himself so the compact would hold.

s12.text: He says the original was lost in a slide year the village could not have survived, and the reasons were good then.

s13.text: They are not defensible now: the village paid iron for a right that is only his bodily tax, which ends only with his death or the relic's public breaking.

s14.text: She still cannot settle what she owes him for raising, craft, and the lie that kept the grain coming, and the rite is days away.

s15.text: To stay and work the truth risks a late or doubtful presentation; to carry the piece as unread spends the recovery on a fraud she now owns.

s16.text: She presents the forged relic and the thin tithe to the Hold's steward, who accepts both without testing inner authenticity, and the compact stands for a year.

s17.text: That night she tells Orren, as a reading of metal rather than a verdict, that she knows the weld, the false weight, and the levy.

s18.text: She will not break the piece or tell the Hold, will not keep the lie after he dies, will work the winter because the hamlet cannot spare a smith, and will leave when the pass opens.

s19.text: He names the old reasons again and does not ask to be forgiven, and she does not grant that those reasons still hold.

s20.text: Orren keeps paying the levy in his body, Willa pays the household that raised her, and the village keeps its grain-right without knowing the protection will die with him.

s21.text: In the morning they share work at the anvil that is no longer the same home, and she watches a true bar bring the balance-arm level.

plot_summary_short:
False Weight is a fantasy screenplay set in Highkettle, a poor late-iron-age mountain village. Each midwinter the village must present a metal relic and a tithe of iron to the valley Hold. Failure means the Hold closes the pass and withholds winter grain for a year. The Hold does not test authenticity unless the object is publicly challenged or broken. Twenty-one days before the rite, raiders steal the relic from the village chest. The hamlet sends Willa, grown apprentice of master smith Orren, to walk the winter pass on foot and recover it, because Orren cannot cross and no one else can be spared.

The crossing costs days and stamina. She takes the relic from the sleeping camp by craft and kills no one. The return frostbites her hands. Six days before the rite she weighs the piece and finds a forty-year forgery: it holds the compact only while Orren pays a hidden bodily levy bound into the weld, ending only with his death or a public breaking. She cannot settle what she owes him. She presents the forged relic and the thin tithe; the steward accepts both and the year is bought. That night she names the weld, will keep silent, will work the winter, and will leave when the pass opens. He repeats the old reasons and is not forgiven. They return to work that is no longer home.
plot_summary_long:
False Weight is a fantasy screenplay set in a secondary world at a late-iron-age, pre-print level of technology. The story is confined to Highkettle, a poor mountain-locked village; the forge-house where its smiths live and work; the winter pass; a hungry camp on the far slope; and the midwinter presentation ground below the valley Hold. Highkettle keeps its right to use the pass and to receive winter grain only by a yearly compact with the Hold. At midwinter the village must present a metal relic kept for that purpose, together with a tithe of the year's iron. If it fails, the Hold closes the pass and withholds grain for one year. The Hold does not test whether the relic is authentic unless the object is publicly challenged or broken. Magic exists only as binding: a named living person pays a concrete bodily or material cost, and the binding never solves a problem without creating a worse one. A relic that is not the original object continues to hold the compact only while a living smith pays a hidden levy bound into the piece when it was forged. That levy cannot be transferred, paused, or paid off except by the bound smith's death or by publicly breaking the relic. Ordinary heat, flux, weight, and quench apply; no metal is inherently magical. The high passes in the three weeks before midwinter can be walked but exact a physiological cost, and the village can afford no mounts or guides. There is no prophecy and no destined person. The screenplay follows Willa, a grown blacksmith's apprentice, who is sent to recover a stolen relic and who must also settle what she owes her master, Orren. Two threads run together: the task of getting the relic accepted before midwinter, and the household question of what she owes the house that raised her.

Twenty-one days before the rite, in the morning, Willa and Orren weigh thin stock for the unfinished tithe on the forge floor. The tithe is already too thin. What she owes him for raising and for her craft remains unnamed and is paid only in work. That night raiders from poorer slopes, people the Hold's protection does not cover, take the relic from the village chest and leave the unfinished tithe-iron, which is too heavy for them to carry. The next morning the hamlet sends Willa after the relic because Orren cannot make the winter crossing and the tithe is still short. The village is too poor to buy a replacement, hire fighters, or meet a punitive extra tithe, and it can spare only the apprentice.

From the twentieth day to the fourteenth, Willa walks the winter pass on foot. The crossing spends days and stamina she cannot spare. On the fourteenth night she enters the raiders' camp on the far slope, takes the relic by weight and craft while the band sleeps, and kills no one. The raiders remain hungry and never become an army. The return, from the fourteenth day to the sixth, frostbites her hands and spends the hours in which Orren might have spoken first.

Six days before the rite, in the evening, before sleep, she weighs the recovered piece. The balance and the visible weld show that the object is a forty-year forgery of Orren's making, already holding the compact by a levy bound to him. She keeps that reading inside the house. That night she takes it to Orren. He admits the weld and the levy bound to himself.

On the fifth day the old reasons fail against present fact: the levy ends only with his death or a public breaking of the piece. On the fourth day she finds she cannot settle the debt. Keeping the piece spends the recovery on a fraud she now owns; exposing it spends the recovery and forfeits the year. On the third day she partitions the unpaid costs: silence now, winter labor because Highkettle cannot spare a smith, and leaving when the pass opens in spring.

On midwinter day she presents the forged relic and the thin tithe at the presentation ground. The Hold's steward accepts both without an inner test. The compact stands for one bought year. The village keeps its grain-right and remains ignorant that the protection will die with Orren. The Hold renews last year's terms on a forgery it did not examine.

That night, back at the forge-house, she tells him she has read the weld, the false weight, and the levy. She will not break the piece, will not tell the Hold or the village, will not keep the lie after he dies, will work the winter, and will leave at the spring opening of the pass. He names the old reasons for the forty-year kindness and the present lie and does not ask to be forgiven. She does not grant that the reasons still hold.

The morning after the rite they return to shared work that is no longer the same household. She sets a true bar on the balance and watches the arm come level. Orren continues to pay the hidden bodily levy in the same house, no longer master of a shared home. Willa is a knowing accomplice for one winter and will lose the forge-house that raised her when the pass opens. No one is redeemed and no one is destroyed.
